title: The Cloud of Unknowing (14th century)
hook: an anonymous English guide: God is reached by love, not by thinking

segments.voice: Yesterday, centering prayer: one sacred word, and consent to his presence. Today, the old book those monks leaned on.

A swimming manual has never kept anyone afloat. A list of reasons to love someone is not the love. Some things can't be reached by thinking. Somewhere in England, in the 1300s, a writer with no name sat down to teach a young person how to pray, and made exactly this point about God. The book is short, strange, and funny in places. Its title gives today's word.
screen: `YOU CAN'T THINK YOUR WAY INTO LOVE.` → `ENGLAND, THE 1300S.` → `A WRITER WITH NO NAME.`

segments.voice: The Cloud of Unknowing was written in Middle English, the English of Chaucer's time, by an author who hid his name on purpose. Some readers guess he was a priest, perhaps a Carthusian monk. Nobody knows. First, the two clouds. When you turn toward God, he says, you find a darkness between you and God, a cloud of unknowing, that your mind can't get through. So you put all your thoughts, even good ones, beneath you in a cloud of forgetting. Second, the key. God can't be reached by thinking, he says, but God can be reached by love. He puts it in two halves: by love God may be gotten and held, but by thought never. The mind can know about God. Only love can touch God. Third, the dart. In the cloud, you send up what he calls a sharp dart of longing love. Keep it short: one word, even one syllable, like God, or love, fastened to your heart. A short prayer, he says, pierces heaven. His picture: someone whose house is on fire doesn't make a speech. They shout one word: fire. Fourth, the humor. He warns against people who strain so hard at prayer that they pull strange faces and twist themselves about. Relax, he says. Don't force it. These last two weeks walked through ways of praying: contemplation, lectio divina, the examen, imagination, the Hours, Compline, the Jesus Prayer, a kitchen, a sacred word, and now a cloud. Tomorrow, a saint builds a castle.
screen: `A CLOUD OF UNKNOWING ABOVE.` · `BY LOVE, NOT BY THOUGHT.` · `A SHARP DART OF LONGING LOVE.` · `DON'T STRAIN. DON'T FORCE IT.` · then, large: `SHORT PRAYER PIERCES HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Let your thoughts drift down beneath you, even the good ones. If you pray, choose one word, God or love, and send it upward, short and whole, whenever you feel the pull, with no explaining. If you don't pray, send the word toward whatever you love most, and let the word do the loving.
Unknowing. The darkness between you and God that thinking can't get through, taught by an anonymous English guide from the 1300s who said God can be held only by love. Today's word.
Your line: by love, not thought. Two weeks of ways of praying, done.

howItsDone: Some Catholics read The Cloud of Unknowing as a guide to silent, wordless prayer, repeating a single short word like God or love as a movement of the heart, and it underlies modern methods such as centering prayer.

notes: All lines from the Cloud are paraphrased (the well-known 'by love may he be gotten and holden; but by thought never' is in modernized editions whose exact wording varies); the screen line 'SHORT PRAYER PIERCES HEAVEN' is a paraphrase of ch. 37–38. Confirm chapter numbers.
The 'fire' illustration: the Cloud itself uses the image of someone crying out 'fire' in a single word (ch. 37); confirm.
Authorship: anonymous; a Carthusian or a country priest are common scholarly guesses. Stated as uncertain.
Humor about straining (strange faces and bodily contortions): paraphrased from the chapters on false contemplatives; confirm the images are in the text.
